newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Opposition protests jam Belgrade anew.
newsitem.headline: Opposition protests jam Belgrade anew.

text.p: Thousands of Serbian opposition supporters blocked central Belgrade on Friday on the 54th day of protests against poll fraud which they say cost them of election victories in major cities last November.

Police were fighting a losing battle to divert traffic from the city centre to prevent opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition supporters from using their vehicles to cause a major traffic jam during the after-work rush hour, witnesses said.

Hundreds of riot police were also present in the streets, raising tensions in the city, hours after persistent students persuaded them to dismantle security cordons and let protesters march in defiance of a ban imposed last month.
Zajedno, protesting against annulment of their victory in November's local elections in Belgrade and 13 other major cities, have started using traffic jams as a new ploy to irritate the authorities.

"We have no dispute with the police, they are also our police -- but we are in conflict with a regime which has stolen our votes," Vuk Draskovic, a Zajedno leader, told some 25,000 people assembled in a central square.

Protesters were expected to be joined soon by a delegation of U.S. congressmen who arrived in Belgrade on Friday to press home the message to President Slobodan Milosevic that he must respect democratic processes in Serbia.
Racheting up pressure on Milosevic, the Contact Group on ex-Yugoslavia meets in Brussels on Saturday amid expectations the five nations will seek to find a common stance on Serbia.
"I have the impression that they are going to try to get a unified position," one NATO source said. "They will probably come out with a fairly strong statement."
The European Union called on Milosevic on Thursday to accept opposition victories and embrace democracy and human rights.

"Only reform directed towards full democratisation and liberalisation of the political and economic system, in dialogue with the opposition, as well as respect for human rights ... will allow for the full integration of Yugoslavia into the international community," it said in a statement.

Federal Yugoslavia, which comprises only Serbia and tiny Montenegro, has been isolated internationally since 1992 when U.N. sanctions were imposed to punish it for fomenting the war in Bosnia. Most sanctions were lifted in 1996.

But Belgrade has yet to be readmitted to the United Nations or key financial institutions like the World Bank, blocking major credits and investment desperately needed by Yugoslavia to rebuild its wrecked economy.
It must improve its bad human rights record before rejoining those institutions, Western officials say.
Remaining so far deaf and mute to the calls, Milosevic, backed only by his police, stood alone in the apparent pursuit of total control of the country.

He has been abandoned by part of the army, the Orthodox Church and on Friday even by his normally staunch allies at the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences. Even his Socialist Party was reportedly split into moderates and hardliners.
Friday's police presence showed the security forces were employing different tactics against Zajedno supporters than against students.

The joy felt earlier in the day over the way the riot police had backed off from a 12-hour standoff with students, abandoning their cordons and prompting opposition revelling in the streets, proved short-lived.
Milosevic conceded on Wednesday that Zajedno had won the election in Serbia's second largest city Nis.
But Zajedno leaders vowed protests would continue until all their claims were met.
The United States said on Thursday that Milosevic's recognition of Zajedno's victory in Nis did not go far enough and he could not win world applause by "dribbling out minor concessions".

U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum began a trip to The Hague, Brussels, Sarajevo and Zagreb to discuss issues pertaining to former Yugoslavia including the political crisis in Serbia. His itinerary deliberately excluded Belgrade.

Paul Poulade, a senior French Foreign Ministry official, was in Belgrade to urge Milosevic to heed confirmation by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) of the opposition's victories.
Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos was due on Sunday to try to ease tensions between Milosevic and the opposition parties.
